title: After getting some feedback from you all, the shader now can be turned off.
author: Mekkablood
selftext:
Some loved it, some hated it, so why not give people a choice? You can see it off towards the end of this video. Also the game is a bit quicker paced than the video shows, it's just not easy getting footage while moving fast side to side. Just build a mech out of trash and get your revenge. [https://store.steampowered.com/app/5541720/Gutter\_Scrap/?beta=0](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5541720/Gutter_Scrap/?beta=0)

This was created in Opus 5.5. Just started small with one character model then branched off into more models, then a single level, then more etc. The key is to dial in your look then replicate. One shots seem to be worse thing you can try. No mcp's all models were done directly by Opus.

replies.author: Deadbringer
replies.body:
Reminds me of when a buddy was making a small VR title and needed me to test it since he had no VR. It was the most nauseating VR experience I have had.


See, my friend enjoyed making small retro titles with the PS1 aesthetic. Problem is those shaders are based on the camera position, so the tiniest head movement made the whole world ripple and shift. And moresso, the shaders were not meant for dual viewports so each eye had its own PS1 artifacting.

Or in short, while some effects are neat and honors certain media, they do not necessarily work when you change the way that media is experienced. When you gain a new perspective on the world, leave the artifacts behind, decouple them from the new perspective. Or like you said, make them world aligned.

comments.author: OneManGameStudio76
comments.body:
The shader toggle is smart. Visual consistency matters more than a specific effect, and letting players adjust it reduces friction.

For the Opus workflow: are the models coming out with clean topology, or are you doing cleanup in Blender before importing? I've seen AI mesh generators produce heavy geometry that breaks physics or look bad under dynamic lighting. If the silhouettes hold up without retopology, that's a huge time saver.

replies.author: Mekkablood
replies.body: That's the beauty of having Opus do it instead of working with an external program. Outside of the issue of models sharing the same space(easily fixed) everything is perfect in that regard, I've never had a single issue from bad uv's doing it this way, no issues with bad animation(from bad topology), and the performance is exceptional.

comments.author: TylerDurden1985
comments.body:
A great way to let a toddler explore new things is to just give them some tools in a safe space and let them have at it.  Finger painting is a great example of this.  You can lock a toddler in a room with a canvas and a bunch of paint and at the end of the day you have a lot of paint on that canvas, and maybe even something you want to hang on the fridge.  All around a great learning experience, and fun times had all around.  No one would think this controversial.  It's not art, there's no actual feeling being evoked from it (intentionally), outside of the joy it brings those parents.  But no one cares, that's not the point, this was after all, a fun learning experience and a happy memory for all.

The problems only arise when an exceptionally delusional parent thinks this splatter canvas is a sign that their child is the next Van Gogh.  Some of those parents may even get more egregious and try to sell that canvas, truly believing it's a special piece that everyone is going to want to experience.  

Now imagine all of a sudden we had tools that let a toddler slap a button and fling paint at a canvas, and it never makes a mess.  It's totally safe and cheap and now everyone is doing it.  All of a sudden there's people clamouring outside of every art gallery within a 50 mile radius trying to sell their shlock, 100% convinced that if they could only get more people to look at it, it would be a huge hit.
